newsitem.title: USA: Uptick in US July PPI won't obscure benign picture.
newsitem.headline: Uptick in US July PPI won't obscure benign picture.

text.p: U.S. producer prices may show their first increase in seven months during July, but economists said any rise should be subdued and insufficient to rouse relatively dormant inflation jitters.
Wholesale finished goods prices fell for a record sixth consecutive month in June and have remained virtually unchanged on a year-over-year basis.
Some economists expected the July report to contain a healthy rise in core crude goods -- goods at the early stage of the production process that exclude the food and energy sectors.
But they said such a development would represent a sole black spot in an otherwise overwhelmingly benign inflation environment.

"I would expect some increases to be visible in core crude goods," said Dana Johnson, managing director and head of economic research at First Chicago Capital Markets, citing recent gains in industrial commodity prices.
"That could remind people that there is a little strength brewing in the background, but it's nothing that will be very alarming."
Economists polled by Reuters expect a 0.1 percent rise in both headline and core producer price readings when the July report is released by the Labor Department on Wednesday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.

In June prices declined 0.1 percent overall and rose by 0.1 percent when the volatile food and energy sectors were excluded. Intermediate goods prices, which were unchanged in June after a 0.2 percent decline in May, could bounce back slightly in July, economists said. But even at this stage of the "pipeline," year-over-year figures offer little reason for concern.
"Even if you go back in the pipeline we're still seeing negligible inflationary pressures on the goods side of the economy," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
Increased competition and a steady strengthening of the dollar were both cited as reasons for the stellar behavior of prices at both the producer and consumer levels.

Economists said the Federal Reserve will keep a close eye on pipeline producer prices for signs of looming price pressures on the finished goods side, but said it would take several months of worsening price reports to spark policymakers to action.
"It's pretty well recognized that inflation at the moment is not a problem," said David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A. Inc.
